request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Banquet hall team leader, female, 8th year

[Earlier in the interview]

Interviewee: Before the takeover, our banquet hall didn’t really have any manuals. Experienced staff trained the new ones, and everything came down to working it out for yourself. Back then I had a lot of my own ways of doing things. There was an old professor who held his birthday banquet with us every year. His teeth weren’t good, so each time I’d quietly ask the kitchen to make his portion a bit softer and cut it a bit smaller. He never had to ask. One year, at his eightieth birthday, he’d had a little to drink, took my hand and said, young lady, you’re more attentive than my own children. After that, his family asked for me by name every time they booked a banquet, and I even won the group’s Service Star award because of it. In the first month after the takeover, out of old habit, I swapped a guest’s glass for a slightly bigger one. The inspector saw it and wrote it up on the checklist: deviation from standard. That month my appraisal score was the lowest in the whole team.

[Later in the interview]

Interviewer: After the hotel was taken over, how did your work change?

Interviewee: Now everything’s standardised. Which hand to pour water with, how to fold the napkins, which words to say when serving a dish: it’s all written into the manual, and we’re assessed on it every quarter. The new brand calls it internationalisation: whichever city’s branch a guest goes to, the experience is the same. Now every event in the banquet hall follows the procedure. There are fewer mistakes and far fewer complaints. The inspector comes every month, and our scores have always been near the top. Last quarter our banquet hall was even named a model unit for standardisation by the group, and the certificate is hanging by the door of the service pantry. We long-serving staff, to be honest, adapted even faster than the young ones. Now it doesn’t matter who’s on duty. You just follow the manual.

response.thinking:
Okay, let's start by looking at the interviewee's details. She's a banquet hall team leader with 8 years of experience. The passage has two parts: earlier and later in the interview.

In the earlier part, she talks about the pre-takeover era where there were no manuals, and she had her own ways of doing things. She mentions a specific incident with the old professor, which shows her personalized service. But after the takeover, she had a problem when she swapped a glass, leading to a low appraisal score. This seems to highlight the shift from personal methods to standardized procedures.

In the later part, she explains how the takeover led to standardization. Everything is now in a manual, and they're assessed quarterly. She mentions the benefits like fewer mistakes and complaints, and the team's recognition. She also notes that long-serving staff adapted quickly, and now the service is consistent regardless of who's on duty.

For coding, I need first-order codes. Let's see. The first part talks about personal service and the incident with the professor. So maybe "Personalized Service Approach" with the quote about the professor's teeth. Then, the takeover leading to standardization, so "Standardization Implementation" with the quote about the manual. The negative experience with the inspector and low score could be "Manual Compliance Pressure" with the deviation from standard quote. The later part mentions benefits like fewer complaints and the model unit recognition, so "Improved Consistency and Recognition" with the certificate quote. Also, the adaptation of experienced staff, "Experienced Staff Adaptation" with the part about long-serving staff adapting faster. Lastly, the shift from personal methods to standardization, "Shift from Personal Methods to Standardization" with the manual and internationalisation quote.

Interpretation: She's discussing the transition from personalized service to standardized procedures post-takeover, highlighting both challenges and benefits like consistency and recognition.

Tone: Mixed, because there are both negative aspects (pressure from compliance) and positive outcomes (recognition and consistency).

Confidence: High, around 95, since the quotes clearly support the codes and interpretation.
